chapter.name: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System

questions.q: Under universal adult franchise in India, from what age does a citizen have the right to vote?
questions.a: Every Indian citizen aged 18 and above has the right to vote.

questions.q: The chapter says the word 'universal' in 'universal adult franchise' carries a special meaning. What does it convey?
o: Every adult citizen may vote, whatever her caste, religion, gender, education or income
Every person living in India, whether a citizen or not, may vote in every single election
A registered voter may cast her vote at any polling booth anywhere in the country
Every citizen, including a child, has a say in elections through a guardian's vote
questions.a: It conveys that every Indian citizen aged 18 and above has the right to vote irrespective of caste, creed, race, religion, gender, education or income.

questions.q: India changed the minimum age for voting from 21 to 18 in 1988. Four citizens, all registered in their own constituencies, give their ages on the day of an election. Which of them could vote at an election held just after the change but could NOT have voted at one held just before it?
questions.a: Sunanda, aged 19: she is below the old minimum of 21 but above the new minimum of 18. Gopal (24) and Hamida (21) could vote under both rules, and Mehul (17) under neither.

questions.q: True or False? 'Under universal adult franchise, only citizens who can read and write have the right to vote.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Every Indian citizen aged 18 and above has the right to vote irrespective of caste, creed, race, religion, gender, education, income and so on, so a citizen who cannot read or write also has the vote.
s: States the verdict: False
Explains that every citizen aged 18 and above may vote irrespective of education (and of caste, religion, gender or income)

questions.q: Rekha, a citizen aged 45, moved from Lucknow to Pune last month. Her name is on the voter list only in her old constituency in Lucknow. (a) On polling day, can she vote at a booth in Pune? Give the rule from the chapter. (b) Her son, who is 17 years and 11 months old on polling day, wants to vote too. Can he? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) No. To exercise the right to vote, a person must be registered as a voter in her constituency; Rekha is registered in Lucknow, not in Pune. (b) No. Only citizens aged 18 and above have the right to vote, and he is still under 18 on polling day.
s: (a) No, with the rule that a voter must be registered in her own constituency
(b) No, because the right to vote begins at 18 and he is under 18

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Under universal adult franchise, the vote of every Indian voter has equal value.
Reason (R): All the local elections in villages and cities are also based on universal franchise, under Article 326 of the Constitution.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. R tells us which elections rest on universal franchise; A rests on the rule that every adult citizen gets one vote and all votes have equal value.

questions.q:
Each person in Column I is turned away at a polling booth. Match each with the rule from the chapter in Column II that applies.
Column I: 1. Ankit, 17, comes along to vote with his elder sister  2. Lata is registered in Indore but tries to vote at a booth in Bhopal  3. Mohan brings his father's voter card to vote for his ailing father  4. A citizen found guilty of a serious crime asks to vote
Column II: P. No one can vote on another's behalf  Q. A voter must be registered in her own constituency  R. One is barred from voting if found guilty of certain serious crimes  S. Only citizens aged 18 and above have the right to vote
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Ankit = only citizens aged 18 and above may vote; Lata = a voter must be registered in her own constituency; Mohan = no one can vote on another's behalf; the convicted citizen = barred for certain serious crimes.

questions.q: Farhan says: 'Article 326 of the Constitution means that everyone living in India can vote in the Lok Sabha, state assembly and village and city elections.' Is he right? Give your verdict, then say what he has got right and what he has got wrong.
questions.a: Partly right. Right: Article 326 makes elections to the Lok Sabha, to the legislative assembly of every state and union territory, and all local elections in villages and cities rest on universal franchise. Wrong: the vote belongs to Indian citizens aged 18 and above, not to everyone living in India; and even an adult citizen must be registered as a voter in her constituency, while one found guilty of certain serious crimes is barred.
s: Verdict: partly right
Confirms the elections Article 326 covers: Lok Sabha, the assemblies of states and union territories, and local elections in villages and cities
Corrects 'everyone living in India': only citizens aged 18 and above who are registered in their constituency and not barred for serious crimes

questions.q: According to the chapter, about what share of Indians were allowed to vote before Independence?
questions.a: Around 13 per cent of Indians were allowed to vote before Independence, and franchise was not universal.

questions.q: The chapter names Switzerland as a country where women won the right to vote late. In which year were women in Switzerland given the vote?
questions.a: Women in Switzerland were given the right to vote only in 1971.

questions.q:
Match each reason for universal adult franchise in Column I, from the chapter's mindmap, with what it means in Column II.
Column I: 1. Power to determine one's future  2. Everyone is equal  3. Elected representatives answerable to the electorate  4. Fosters civic engagement
Column II: P. People can vote them out in elections  Q. People participate in solving problems in their area  R. People decide what type of future they want and who can best represent them  S. No discrimination based on caste, creed, sex, education or wealth
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Power to determine one's future = people decide their future and who represents them; everyone is equal = no discrimination; representatives answerable = people vote them out; civic engagement = people help solve problems in their area.

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What was India's literacy rate in 1947, according to the chapter? (b) What was the literacy rate among women in 1947? (c) Some people argued that only literate people should get the vote. Which reason in the chapter's mindmap would such a rule have gone against?
questions.a: (a) About 14 per cent. (b) About 8 per cent. (c) 'Everyone is equal', which means no discrimination based on education (accept also 'everyone's voice matters': all can take part in deciding the nation's future).
s: (a) States about 14 per cent
(b) States about 8 per cent
(c) Names 'everyone is equal' (no discrimination by education) or 'everyone's voice matters'

questions.q: After a ward election in Kochi, residents form a group with their newly elected councillor. Every Sunday they meet to plan how to clear the blocked drains in their lane, and many of them volunteer to do the work. Which reason in the chapter's mindmap for universal adult franchise does this show most directly?
o: Elected representatives are answerable to the electorate
It gives people power to determine their future
questions.a: It fosters civic engagement: the chapter's mindmap says people participate in solving problems in their area.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In India, women had voting rights from the very beginning.
Reason (R): In 1947 only about 8 per cent of Indian women could read and write.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The chapter credits a progressive constitutional vision and deep democratic values rooted in India's ancient traditions for women's vote; low literacy among women is a separate fact, and was even used by some to argue for limiting the vote.

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Udaipur studies women in local government. The chapter says India has 3.1 million elected representatives in more than 250,000 local government bodies, and 1.3 million of them are women. The group also visits the municipal council of a nearby town (illustrative figures), which has 60 elected members, of whom 24 are women. Riya concludes: 'Women now hold half the seats in local government across India, and our town council proves it.'
(a) Through what kind of franchise does the chapter say all these local representatives are elected?
(b) What percentage of India's elected local representatives are women? Give one decimal place.
(c) What percentage of the town council's members are women?
(d) Using (b) and (c), judge Riya's conclusion.
questions.a: (a) Universal adult franchise; they are all democratically elected through it. (b) 1.3 / 3.1 x 100 = about 41.9 per cent. (c) 24 / 60 x 100 = 40 per cent. (d) Riya is not right: both figures are below half (nationally about 1.8 million of the 3.1 million are men), and one town cannot prove a national figure anyway. What the data do show is that about two in every five local representatives are women, a large share.
s: (a) Universal adult franchise
(b) About 41.9 per cent (1.3 / 3.1 x 100)
(d) Judges the claim wrong: both shares are below 50 per cent and one town cannot prove a national figure; notes women are still about two in five

questions.q: For how many Lok Sabha constituencies did India vote in the general election of 2024?
questions.a: 543 constituencies of the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Which voting facility does the chapter say was offered for the FIRST time in 2024?
o: Elderly voters and persons with disabilities could vote from home
Every voter in the country, wherever she lived, could vote by post
Voters had to show a voter ID card so that proxy voting would end
Voters with poor eyesight marked an 'X' on a ballot paper in braille
questions.a: In 2024, for the first time, the elderly and people with disabilities could cast their votes from home. Postal voting was only for a specific category of voters, and voter IDs date from T.N. Seshan's reforms.

questions.q: The chapter uses two comparisons to show how large and complex India is. (a) India's population of eligible voters is about how many times the population of the United Kingdom? (b) In area, India is about how many times larger than France?
questions.a: (a) About fifteen times. (b) About six times.
s: (a) Fifteen times the population of the United Kingdom
(b) Six times larger than France

questions.q: True or False? 'About two out of every three eligible voters cast their vote in the 2024 elections.' Give the verdict and show how you know.
questions.a: True. The chapter says about 34 per cent of eligible voters did not vote in 2024, so about 100 - 34 = 66 per cent did vote, which is about two out of every three.
s: States the verdict: True
Uses the 34 per cent who did not vote to get about 66 per cent who voted, about two in three

questions.q: Over 968 million voters were eligible in the 2024 general election, and about 34 per cent of eligible voters did not vote. Roughly how many eligible voters stayed away?
questions.a: About 329 million: 34 per cent of 968 million is 0.34 x 968 = 329.12 million. 639 million is the number who did vote.

questions.q: An election team in a hill district of Uttarakhand (illustrative) lists voters who might miss polling day: (a) Dolma, 91, who is bedridden; (b) Kailash, who is blind; (c) Rekha, who uses a wheelchair, and whose booth is at the top of a flight of steps; (d) the 14 voters of a hamlet a full day's walk from the nearest road. For (a), (b) and (c), name the measure from the chapter that helps each person vote. For (d), say what the chapter says electoral officials do, and explain why the Election Commission goes to such lengths for so few voters.
questions.a: (a) Home voting: in 2024, for the first time, the elderly and persons with disabilities could vote from home. (b) Braille-enabled voter cards, one of the assistive technologies. (c) An app-based request for assistance, such as a wheelchair or a ramp. (d) Electoral officials travel to remote locations; under universal adult franchise every eligible citizen has the right to vote, and the aim is that no voter is left behind, so even a handful of voters is reached (the chapter shows a polling station set up for a single woman voter).
s: (a) Home voting for the elderly and persons with disabilities (first offered in 2024)
(b) Braille-enabled voter cards
(c) App-based request for a wheelchair or ramp
(d) Officials travel to remote places, because every eligible citizen must be able to vote and no voter is left behind

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Election Commission's efforts to make sure no voter is left behind.
I. In 2024, postal voting was available to every voter in the country.
II. Electoral officials travel to remote locations so that citizens there can vote.
III. Braille-enabled voter cards are among the assistive technologies the chapter names.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements II and III are correct. Statement I is wrong: in 2024 postal voting was available only for a specific category of voters.

questions.q:
The election office of a district in Arunachal Pradesh (illustrative figures) has one spare polling team for polling day, and two places want it. Place A is a mountain village of 38 voters, two days' trek from the nearest booth; at the last election only 5 of them made the trip and voted. Place B is a town ward with 400 voters who are elderly or persons with disabilities; 260 of them did not vote last time, and 180 of these have now asked to vote from home.
(a) What percentage of Place A's voters did not vote at the last election? Give one decimal place.
(b) What percentage of Place B's 400 voters did not vote last time?
(c) Name the measure from the chapter that each place needs.
(d) The team can serve only one place this time. Which should it serve? Justify your choice with your figures and the aim the chapter gives for these measures.
questions.a: (a) 38 - 5 = 33 did not vote; 33 / 38 x 100 = about 86.8 per cent. (b) 260 / 400 x 100 = 65 per cent. (c) Place A: officials travelling to a remote location (taking the booth to the voters); Place B: home voting for the elderly and persons with disabilities. (d) Either choice earns the mark if justified with the data and the aim that no voter is left behind. Place B: the team could add up to 180 votes against at most 33 in Place A. Place A: a far larger share is shut out (86.8 against 65 per cent) and its voters have no other way to reach a booth, and the chapter shows booths set up even for a single voter. A strong answer adds that the place not served must still be planned for.
s: (a) About 86.8 per cent (33 of 38)
(b) 65 per cent (260 of 400)
(c) Place A: officials travel to the remote location; Place B: home voting
(d) A justified decision that weighs the numbers (180 against 33) and the shares (86.8 against 65 per cent) against the aim that no voter is left behind

questions.q: In the Suryodaya School class representative election, who was appointed the Election Officer?
o: Ms Sheeba, a teacher from the next class
Ahmed, one of the three candidates
Neha, a student of the class
questions.a: The class teacher, Ms. Usha, was appointed the Election Officer to make sure the election was fair, transparent and followed the rules.

questions.q: What does a NOTA vote do, according to the chapter?
o: It lets a voter reject every candidate, without changing the result
It cancels the whole election if it gets more votes than any candidate
It lets a voter give a second vote to her own favourite candidate
It is treated as an invalid ballot, just like an unmarked ballot paper
questions.a: NOTA (None Of The Above) lets a voter reject all the candidates; it does not change the result but sends a message that voters want better choices.

questions.q: The 10th-century Uttaramerur inscriptions describe how representatives were selected. On what were the names of eligible candidates written before they were placed in a sealed pot?
questions.a: The names were written on fragments of palm leaves and placed in a pot, which was then sealed.

questions.q: (a) What is meant by a secret ballot? (b) Give one reason why it is important in an election.
questions.a: (a) A way of voting in which no one knows who voted for whom. (b) It keeps the vote private and fair, so each voter can choose freely without fear of or pressure from anyone.
s: (a) No one knows who voted for whom
(b) It keeps voting private and fair, so voters choose freely without pressure

questions.q:
Class 8C of a school in Ranchi (illustrative) holds its class representative election in the Suryodaya way. The class teacher, Mr. Das, is the Election Officer. Each of the 40 students gets a ballot paper with three names and marks an 'X' next to one. Sana, who cannot see, is given a ballot paper in braille. Mr. Das seals the box until the count, which Ms. Roy from Class 8D comes to watch. The count reads: Pallavi 16, Tarun 13, Zubin 9, and 2 ballot papers carry no mark.
(a) How many valid votes were cast?
(b) Who wins, and by how many votes over the runner-up?
(c) What happens to the 2 ballot papers that carry no mark?
(d) Why was Sana given a ballot paper in braille?
questions.a: (a) 16 + 13 + 9 = 38 valid votes (40 ballots minus the 2 unmarked). (b) Pallavi wins with the most votes, 16 - 13 = 3 votes ahead of Tarun. (c) They are declared invalid and are not counted for any candidate, as with the unmarked ballot at Suryodaya. (d) So that she too can cast her own vote, secretly, like every other voter; every voter must be able to vote.
s: (a) 38 valid votes
(b) Pallavi, by 3 votes over Tarun
(c) Declared invalid and counted for no one
(d) So that she can cast her own secret vote like everyone else; no voter is left out

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A voter in India who is not satisfied with any of the candidates can still use her vote to send a message.
Reason (R): India offers the option NOTA, None Of The Above, which allows voters to reject all the candidates.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: by choosing NOTA she rejects all the candidates, which does not change the result but tells everyone that voters want better choices.

questions.q: In one important way, the 10th-century Uttaramerur process was DIFFERENT from the Suryodaya class election. Which one?
o: At Uttaramerur, names were drawn at random from a pot, so no one cast a vote
At Uttaramerur, the whole process was carried out in secret, away from the public
At Uttaramerur, there was no step at all to guard against cheating
At Uttaramerur, voters marked an 'X' next to a name on a palm leaf
questions.a: At Uttaramerur, a young boy drew the palm leaves at random from the sealed pot, so representatives were selected by lot rather than by votes. The pot was opened in public and the reader showed his empty hands, so it was neither secret nor unguarded.

questions.q: Tara says: 'The Uttaramerur process was more transparent than the Suryodaya election, because at Uttaramerur everything happened in public, while at Suryodaya the votes were cast in secret.' Is she right? Give your verdict and reasons from both processes.
questions.a: Partly right. At Uttaramerur every step was public: the sealed pot was opened in public, a young boy drew the palm leaves at random, and the reader showed his empty hands before reading each name. But at Suryodaya only each student's choice was secret, to keep the vote private and fair; the rest was open: the Election Officer explained the rules, the box stayed sealed until the count, Ms Sheeba from the next class witnessed the count, the invalid ballot was declared and the result announced. So a secret ballot is not a lack of transparency; both processes were transparent in their own way.
s: Verdict: partly right (not fully)
Shows the public steps at Uttaramerur: sealed pot opened in public, random draw, empty hands shown
Shows that at Suryodaya only the choice was secret while the sealed box, witnessed count and announced result were open

questions.q:
Read the statements about who runs elections in India.
I. The Election Commission of India was established in 1950, before the first general elections of 1951-1952.
II. Elections to gram panchayats and urban local bodies are conducted by the Election Commission of India alone, with no other body involved.
III. The Model Code of Conduct was first drawn up by the Election Commission of India in 1991.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement I is correct. Elections to gram panchayats and urban local bodies are managed by the State Election Commissions, working in consultation with the ECI. The Model Code of Conduct was adopted in Kerala in 1960; 1991 is when the ECI became proactive in ensuring it was observed.

questions.q:
Match each officer in Column I with the description in Column II, from the chapter's chart of the structure of the Election Commission of India.
Column I: 1. Chief Election Commissioner  2. Chief Electoral Officer  3. Returning Officer  4. Electoral Registration Officer
Column II: P. Manages the voter list, at district level  Q. Works at the national level, with two Election Commissioners  R. Works at the state or union territory level  S. Conducts the elections, at district level
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Chief Election Commissioner = national level, with two Election Commissioners; Chief Electoral Officer = state or union territory level; Returning Officer = conducts elections; Electoral Registration Officer = manages the voter list.

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) In which years were the first general elections in independent India held? (b) Besides the Lok Sabha, name any two elections that the Election Commission of India conducts. (c) Which bodies manage the elections to gram panchayats and urban local bodies?
questions.a: (a) 1951-1952. (b) Any two of: the Rajya Sabha, the State Legislative Assemblies, the office of the President, the office of the Vice President. (c) The State Election Commissions.
s: (b) Any two of Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, President, Vice President
(c) The State Election Commissions

questions.q: True or False? 'T.N. Seshan, who became Chief Election Commissioner in 1990, brought in voter IDs to eliminate proxy voting.' Give the verdict and name one other reform he brought in.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Seshan brought in voter IDs to eliminate proxy voting. His other reforms were precise rules for campaigning and strict vigilance on spending by candidates.
s: States the verdict: True
Names another Seshan reform: precise campaigning rules or strict vigilance on candidates' spending

questions.q: During assembly elections in Goa (illustrative), four reports reach the district election office. Which one is NOT a breach of the Model Code of Conduct?
o: A candidate holds a peaceful public meeting to explain her plan for the town's water supply
A candidate's workers hand out pressure cookers to voters in a housing colony in return for their votes
A senior government officer speaks at a rally, asking people to vote for the ruling party's candidate
A candidate calls a rival candidate abusive names in a speech at a crowded street-corner meeting
questions.a: The peaceful public meeting to explain a plan is ordinary campaigning with restraint. Gifts in return for votes, government officials campaigning for the ruling party and abusive language against a rival are all breaches the chapter illustrates.

questions.q: The chapter calls the Election Commission of India an independent constitutional body. Explain why its independence from the government of the day matters, using (a) its task of setting election dates, (b) its task of enforcing the Model Code of Conduct, and (c) the purpose for which the chapter says it exists.
questions.a: (a) If the ruling party set the dates it could pick a time that suits itself; an independent body sets them fairly for all. (b) The code has rules the party in government must follow, so that government resources are not used for the election (for example, no new schemes that may influence voters); only a body the government does not control can enforce these rules on the government itself. (c) The ECI is responsible for conducting free and fair elections, which is possible only if no party controls it.
s: (a) Dates set by an independent body cannot be chosen to suit the ruling party
(b) The code binds the party in government (no use of government resources, no new schemes), so the enforcer must be outside its control
(c) Links independence to its purpose of free and fair elections

questions.q: An imaginary island nation asks India for advice on setting up an election body like the Election Commission of India. The island has 4 provinces, each with 5 districts. Using the chapter's chart of the ECI's structure and tasks, answer: (a) who should sit at the national level, and which officer should work for each province; (b) how many district-level officers are needed in all if every district has the same three officers as an Indian district, and what two of them do; (c) which four tasks the national body should take on; (d) the island's ruling party wants its own minister to set election dates and register parties. Give your advice.
questions.a: (a) A Chief Election Commissioner with two Election Commissioners; a Chief Electoral Officer for each province, like a state or union territory. (b) 4 x 5 = 20 districts; 20 x 3 = 60 officers (a District Election Officer, a Returning Officer and an Electoral Registration Officer in each). The Returning Officer conducts the elections and the Electoral Registration Officer manages the voter list. (c) Setting election dates, enforcing a Model Code of Conduct, registering political parties and overseeing the entire electoral process. (d) Advise against it: in India these are tasks of an independent constitutional body, and a ruling party's minister could set dates or register parties to suit itself, so the elections would not be free and fair.
s: (a) Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners; a Chief Electoral Officer per province
(b) 60 district officers (20 districts x 3), with the Returning Officer conducting elections and the Electoral Registration Officer managing the voter list
(c) The four tasks: dates, Model Code of Conduct, registering parties, overseeing the whole process
(d) Advises against it, because these tasks belong to an independent body so that elections stay free and fair

questions.q: What does VVPAT, used with India's electronic voting machines, stand for?
o: Visual Voting Paper Audit and Tracking
Voter Vote Printing And Tracking Record
questions.a: Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail.

questions.q: At a polling station, which polling officer inks the voter's finger, gives her a chit and takes her signature?
questions.a: The second polling officer inks the finger, gives the chit and takes the signature. The first checks the name and ID proof; the third takes the chit and checks the finger.

questions.q:
A Lok Sabha constituency (illustrative figures) has 18,40,000 voters and 1,840 polling stations. To save staff, an official proposes merging 12 small polling stations in a hill area, each serving 60 voters, into 2 larger stations of 360 voters each. Voters in the hills would then walk up to three hours to reach a booth.
(a) On average, how many voters does one polling station in this constituency serve?
(b) If every station has the three polling officers of the chapter's voting process, how many polling officers would the merger save?
(c) Say in one line what each of the three polling officers does.
(d) Which aim of the Election Commission, as the chapter describes it, could the merger work against, and how?
(e) Should the stations be merged? Justify your decision using (b) and (d).
questions.a: (a) 18,40,000 / 1,840 = 1,000 voters. (b) Before: 12 x 3 = 36 officers; after: 2 x 3 = 6; saving 30 officers. (c) The first checks the name on the voter list and the ID proof; the second inks the finger, gives a chit and takes the signature; the third takes the chit and checks the finger. (d) The aim that no voter is left behind: the ECI removes barriers so that every eligible citizen can vote, and officials even travel to remote places; a three-hour walk is a new barrier, especially for the elderly and persons with disabilities, and some of the 720 voters may stay away. (e) Either decision earns the mark if it weighs (b) against (d). Keeping the 12 stations is the stronger answer: 30 officers is a small saving when many people, including teachers, are already deployed, and the chapter shows a polling station set up even for a single voter. An answer for merging must say how the hill voters would still be helped to vote.
s: (a) 1,000 voters per station
(b) 30 officers saved (36 before, 6 after)
(c) The work of the first, second and third polling officers
(d) The aim that no voter is left behind, and how a long walk becomes a barrier
(e) A decision that weighs the 30 officers saved against access for the 720 hill voters

questions.q: (a) What is a VVPAT? (b) Why is its paper record useful?
questions.a: (a) A system that produces a physical paper record, allowing voters to verify that their electronic votes were cast correctly. (b) The paper trail is a backup for verifying and recounting votes if there is a dispute or the electronic system fails.
s: (a) A system that gives a paper record so voters can verify their electronic vote
(b) A backup for verification and recounting in disputes or failures

questions.q: True or False? 'Once the second polling officer has inked her finger, a voter must choose one of the candidates; there is no way left for her to reject them all.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. After the second polling officer, the third polling officer takes her chit and checks her finger, and the NOTA (None Of The Above) option is also available, so she can still reject all the candidates.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: at the third polling officer's stage the NOTA option is available, so she can reject all candidates

questions.q: The 2024 Lok Sabha election used over 1 million polling stations for 543 constituencies. Taking exactly 1 million polling stations, about how many polling stations did one constituency have on average?
questions.a: About 1,840: 10,00,000 / 543 = about 1,841.6 polling stations per constituency.

questions.q:
Read the statements about polling day and voting technology.
I. The first polling officer checks the voter's name on the voter list and her ID proof.
II. 84 Lok Sabha constituencies are reserved for scheduled tribes.
III. India's EVMs and VVPAT systems have been used in Namibia and Bhutan with support from the Election Commission of India.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: 84 constituencies are reserved for scheduled castes, and 47 for scheduled tribes.

questions.q: India uses the 'First-Past-the-Post' electoral system. What does this mean?
o: The candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins
A candidate wins only with more than half of all the votes
The candidate who files her nomination first wins the seat
The largest party in the state chooses each seat's winner
questions.a: The candidate receiving the most votes in a constituency wins, even without securing 50 per cent of the votes.

questions.q: A state legislative assembly (illustrative) has 80 seats. A party or coalition needs a majority of the seats to form the government. What is the smallest number of seats that is a majority here?
questions.a: 41 seats: a majority is more than half of 80, and half of 80 is 40.

questions.q: (a) What is a coalition? (b) When does a coalition form the national government?
questions.a: (a) A group of two or more parties working together. (b) When it wins a majority of the seats in the Lok Sabha; its leader typically becomes the prime minister.
s: (a) A group of two or more parties working together
(b) When it wins a majority of Lok Sabha seats

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What are the members elected to the Lok Sabha called? (b) What are the members elected to a state legislative assembly called? (c) At which level of governance does each of them work?
questions.a: (a) Members of Parliament (MPs). (b) Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs). (c) MPs represent us in the national Parliament; MLAs represent us in the state assembly.
s: (a) Members of Parliament (MPs)
(b) Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs)
(c) MPs at the national level, MLAs at the state level

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After a general election, the single party that wins the most Lok Sabha seats always forms the national government.
Reason (R): A coalition is a group of two or more parties working together.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. The government is formed by the party or coalition that wins a majority of the seats, so if no party has a majority, a coalition of other parties holding a majority can form it. R is the chapter's meaning of a coalition.

questions.q:
Read this illustrative result of a Lok Sabha constituency in Tamil Nadu and answer each part in one line. Candidate K: 3,90,000 votes; Candidate L: 3,60,000 votes; Candidate M: 2,50,000 votes.
(a) Who wins this seat?
(b) What is the winner called once she takes her seat in the Lok Sabha?
(c) How many votes did the three candidates get in all?
(d) Did the winner get more than half of these votes?
(e) Name the electoral system that lets a candidate win in this way.
questions.a: (a) Candidate K, who has the most votes. (b) A Member of Parliament (MP). (c) 3,90,000 + 3,60,000 + 2,50,000 = 10,00,000 votes. (d) No: half of 10,00,000 is 5,00,000, and K got 3,90,000 (39 per cent). (e) First-Past-the-Post.
s: (a) Candidate K
(b) Member of Parliament (MP)
(c) 10,00,000 votes in all
(d) No, 3,90,000 is less than half (5,00,000)
(e) First-Past-the-Post

questions.q:
After assembly elections in a state whose Vidhan Sabha has 60 seats (illustrative figures), the results are: Party X 28 seats, Party Y 19, Party Z 9 and Party W 4. Parties Y and Z announce that they will work together, and Party W then says it will join them. Party X says it should form the government because it is the largest party.
(a) What is the smallest number of seats that makes a majority in this assembly?
(b) Can Party X form the government on its own? Explain using (a).
(c) How many seats do Y and Z hold together, and how many with W? What is such a group of parties called?
(d) Decide which side should form the government, and say who typically becomes the chief minister.
questions.a: (a) 31 seats, more than half of 60. (b) No: 28 is fewer than 31, so X does not have a majority on its own. (c) Y and Z hold 19 + 9 = 28, only equal to X; with W they hold 28 + 4 = 32. A group of two or more parties working together is a coalition. (d) The Y-Z-W coalition, because 32 is a majority (32 is at least 31) and the chapter says the party or coalition with a majority forms the government; being the largest single party is not enough. The leader of this majority typically becomes the chief minister.
s: (a) 31 seats
(b) No, 28 is less than the 31 needed
(c) 28 without W, 32 with W; the group is a coalition
(d) The Y-Z-W coalition forms the government because only it has a majority; its leader typically becomes chief minister

questions.q: How many members of the Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President of India?
questions.a: The President nominates 12 of the 245 members of the Rajya Sabha; the other 233 are elected by the MLAs.

questions.q: The chapter names three challenges facing India's electoral system. Which of these is NOT one of them?
o: Too few polling stations in the cities
The growing influence of money in elections
Voter apathy, particularly in urban areas
questions.a: Too few polling stations in the cities is not one of them. The three challenges the chapter names are the growing influence of money, a significant proportion of candidates with criminal records, and voter apathy, particularly in urban areas.

questions.q: (a) How long is the term of a member of the Rajya Sabha? (b) What part of its members retire every two years?
questions.a: (a) Six years. (b) One-third of its members retire every two years, and new members are elected.
s: (a) Six years
(b) One-third of the members

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Rajya Sabha is never dissolved.
Reason (R): All the members of the Rajya Sabha retire together at the end of every six years.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The Rajya Sabha is the Permanent House and is never dissolved. Each member has a six-year term, but only one-third of the members retire every two years, which is why the House carries on.

questions.q: A student is preparing a fact file on the Rajya Sabha. Help her complete it, one line for each part. (a) The Rajya Sabha has 245 members, of whom the President nominates 12. How many are elected? (b) Who elects these members? (c) What name does the chapter give the Rajya Sabha because it is never dissolved? (d) Which voting system do the electors use?
questions.a: (a) 245 - 12 = 233 members. (b) The elected members of the state legislative assemblies (MLAs), through indirect elections. (c) The Permanent House. (d) The single transferable vote system.
s: (a) 233 elected members
(b) The elected MLAs of the states
(c) The Permanent House
(d) The single transferable vote system

questions.q: Differentiate between the election of members to the Lok Sabha and to the Rajya Sabha under three heads: (a) who casts the votes; (b) the voting system used; (c) what the members are called once elected.
questions.a: (a) Lok Sabha: the voters of each constituency vote directly; Rajya Sabha: the elected members of the state legislative assemblies (MLAs) vote, so it is an indirect election. (b) Lok Sabha: First-Past-the-Post, where the candidate with the most votes wins; Rajya Sabha: the single transferable vote system. (c) No difference: members of both Houses are called Members of Parliament (MPs).
s: (a) Direct vote by the people for the Lok Sabha; vote by elected MLAs (indirect) for the Rajya Sabha
(b) First-Past-the-Post for the Lok Sabha; single transferable vote for the Rajya Sabha
(c) Both are called Members of Parliament (MPs)

questions.q:
Read the statements about the electoral colleges for the President and the Vice President of India.
I. An elected MLA of Puducherry votes in the election of the President but not in that of the Vice President.
II. A nominated member of the Rajya Sabha votes in the election of the Vice President but not in that of the President.
III. An elected member of the Lok Sabha votes in both elections.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three are correct. The President's electoral college has the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected MLAs of the states and of Delhi and Puducherry, but not nominated members. The Vice President's electoral college has the elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament, but no MLAs.

questions.q:
A school in Shillong (illustrative) has 600 students in 20 classes, and each class already elects its own class representative. Two plans are proposed for choosing the school captain. Plan 1: all 600 students vote directly. Plan 2: the 20 class representatives elect the captain.
(a) Which plan is a direct election and which is an indirect one?
(b) Name one office or seat in India that is filled the way Plan 2 works, and say who elects it.
(c) The chapter says the method used to elect the President ensures the support of both the central and the state governments. What is the school-level version of this advantage in Plan 2?
(d) Using a reason from the chapter's mindmap on why universal franchise matters, give one thing Plan 1 offers that Plan 2 does not.
(e) Which plan would you recommend? Justify your choice using (c) and (d).
questions.a: (a) Plan 1 is direct; Plan 2 is indirect. (b) Either: the 233 elected members of the Rajya Sabha, elected by the elected MLAs; or the President, elected by an electoral college of elected MPs and the elected MLAs of the states, Delhi and Puducherry. (c) The captain would have the backing of the representatives of every class, not just of the biggest classes or groups. (d) 'Everyone's voice matters' (or 'power to determine one's future'): every one of the 600 students has a direct say in choosing the captain. (e) Either plan earns the mark if justified: Plan 1 gives every student a direct voice; Plan 2 makes sure the captain has support from every class, and its electors were themselves directly chosen by the students. The answer must weigh one advantage against the other.
s: (a) Plan 1 direct, Plan 2 indirect
(b) Names the Rajya Sabha (elected by MLAs) or the President (electoral college)
(c) The captain has the support of the representatives of every class
(d) Names a mindmap reason such as 'everyone's voice matters': each student gets a direct say
(e) A recommendation that weighs the advantage in (c) against the one in (d)
